newsitem.title: USA: FBI probing passing of U.S. data to Israel - report.
newsitem.headline: FBI probing passing of U.S. data to Israel - report.

text.p: The FBI has opened an investigation to determine whether a senior U.S. government official has been passing highly sensitive information to the Israeli government, the Washington Post reported on Wednesday.

Quoting sources with direct knowledge of the inquiry, the newspaper said the investigation was launched in January after the National Security Agency intercepted a secure communication between a senior Israeli intelligence officer in Washington and a superior in Tel Aviv.
The communication referred to someone codenamed "Mega" and to an attempt to obtain a sensitive American document, according to the report.
The Post said the content of the conversation led U.S. officials to believe that Mega may be someone in the U.S. government who provided information to the Israelis in the past.

The newspaper's sources said the investigation was focusing on U.S. officials who would have had access to the document in question, a secret letter of assurances given by then Secretary of State Warren Christopher to Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat after successful negotiations to withdraw Israeli troops from most of the West Bank city of Hebron.

In the intercepted conversation, according to two unidentified U.S. officials quoted by the Post, the Israeli intelligence officer informed his superior in Tel Aviv that Israeli Ambassador Eliahu Ben Elissar had asked him whether he could obtain a copy of the letter Christopher gave to Arafat on Jan. 16, the day after the Hebron accord was signed.

According to a source who reviewed a copy of the National Security Agency transcript of the conversation, the intelligence officer, speaking in Hebrew, said: "The ambassador wants me to go to Mega to get a copy of this letter."
The source said the supervisor in Tel Aviv rejected the request, saying, "This is not something we use Mega for."

The Post quoted Ambassador Ben Elissar as saying emphatically that his government had not engaged in any improper activity in Washington, denying that he had made such a request or that Israel had a spy inside the U.S. government.
